From segments to a density surface

Source: vignettes/from-segments-to-density.Rmd
from-segments-to-density.Rmd
library(distsamp)

distsamp stops at segments. This vignette starts where vignette("segmenting-narwc-data") ends and passes the output to Distance and dsm. The two places this handoff usually goes wrong are units and the key between segments and detections.

The Distance and dsm chunks are not evaluated. Neither package is a dependency of distsamp, so the vignette builds without them. The code runs once they are installed.

The data is synthetic. narwc-example.csv is generated by data-raw/make-fixture.R. No real NARWC records are distributed with the package or were used to develop it. The fixture has two days, seven tracks, and a few sightings: far too few to fit a detection function or a density surface. The numbers below show the mechanics only; none is a result.

Segment the survey 

path <- system.file("extdata", "narwc-example.csv", package = "distsamp")
dat <- read_narwc(path)
#> `read_narwc()` renamed 2 columns:
#>   LAT_DD  -> LATITUDE
#>   LONG_DD -> LONGITUDE
#> All matched an exact entry in the alias table; `narwc_column_mapping()` returns this, and `quiet = TRUE` silences it.
segs <- segment_survey(dat, seg_length = 5, seed = 1, species = "RIWH")
segs
#> <distsamp_segments>
#>   segments:  20
#>   tracks:    7
#>   total effort: 92.23 km
#>   segment length: median 4.44 km, range 2.22-7.78 km
#>   target length: 5 km   seed: 1
#>   species:   RIWH
#>   detections: 6 (6 with a perpendicular distance, m)

Two tables are used here.

segments holds the sampling units, one row each, with effort and a location:

head(segs$segments[, c("seg_id", "seg_eff", "mid_lat", "mid_lon", "wt_beaufort")])
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   seg_id         seg_eff mid_lat mid_lon wt_beaufort
#>   <chr>            <dbl>   <dbl>   <dbl>       <dbl>
#> 1 2024-04-01_2_1    7.78    43.0   -69             2
#> 2 2024-04-01_2_2    5.56    43.1   -69             2
#> 3 2024-04-01_2_3    3.33    43.1   -69             2
#> 4 2024-04-01_2_4    5.56    43.2   -69             2
#> 5 2024-04-01_4_1    4.44    43.3   -69.1           2
#> 6 2024-04-01_4_2    3.33    43.3   -69.1           2

detections holds one row per sighting, with its perpendicular distance:

segs$detections[, c("seg_id", "SPECCODE", "size", "distance", "side")]
#> # A tibble: 6 × 5
#>   seg_id         SPECCODE  size distance side 
#>   <chr>          <chr>    <dbl>    <dbl> <chr>
#> 1 2024-04-01_2_1 RIWH         1    229   right
#> 2 2024-04-01_2_2 RIWH         2    132.  left 
#> 3 2024-04-01_2_2 RIWH         1    397.  right
#> 4 2024-04-01_4_2 RIWH         3     61.4 left 
#> 5 2024-04-01_4_2 RIWH         2    855.  right
#> 6 2024-04-02_1_3 RIWH         4    160.  left

seg_id is the key between them. Every detection belongs to exactly one segment, and that segment carries the effort the detection was made on.

Match the units

Mismatched units are the most common way to get a density estimate wrong by a factor of 1000.

c(effort = "km", distance = segs$settings$distance_units)
#>   effort distance 
#>     "km"      "m"

seg_eff is in kilometres, because effort accumulates in km. distance defaults to metres, because ALT is in metres (handbook 8.A.1) and aerial cetacean surveys conventionally report perpendicular distances in metres.

There are two options. Work in kilometres throughout:

segs_km <- segment_survey(dat, seg_length = 5, seed = 1, species = "RIWH",
                          distance_units = "km")
segs_km$detections$distance
#> [1] 0.22900000 0.13221321 0.39663963 0.06136037 0.85463963 0.16034753

Or keep metres and pass a conversion factor to Distance as convert_units. For distance in m, effort in km, and area in km², the factor is:

# distance in m, effort in km, area in km^2: m -> km
convert_units <- 0.001

The same factor goes to dsm() as convert.units. State the choice in your methods.

Plot the distances

Look at the distribution before fitting a curve to it.

plot(segs, what = "distances")

Expect a shoulder near zero and a tail that falls away. What you see changes what you fit:

  • A dip in the first bin may not be a sampling artefact. An aircraft cannot see the water directly beneath it. For the Skymaster, handbook 8.A.31 says CETAP-era distances “are actually measured from about 1/8 mile to either side of the survey line”. Use left truncation, ds(left = ...); do not assume the animals were absent.
  • A peak away from zero is what the gamma key function describes. Distance::ds() does not offer it (only hn, hr, and unif); use mrds::ddf(key = "gamma"). A gamma key and left truncation model the same blind spot, so using both counts it twice.
  • A long flat tail calls for stronger truncation.
  • A distance the aircraft could not have seen is a broken record, not a wide detection: a sighting matched to the wrong segment, or a coordinate with a lost sign. The axis stops at the 99th percentile so one such value cannot push every real distance into the first bin. The subtitle reports how many lie beyond it and how large the largest is. If the largest is too far to be a detection, fix it before fitting. ?sighting_distances says where each distance comes from.

The plot says nothing about g(0), the probability of detecting an animal on the track-line. Animals submerged when the aircraft passed leave no trace here. A smooth curve is equally consistent with half of them having been invisible.

Fit a detection function

Distance::ds() takes a data frame with a distance column and, optionally, size and detection covariates. detection_data() builds that table, often called a flatfile:

flat <- detection_data(
  segs,
  area = 5811,                    # square km - yours to supply
  covariates = "wt_beaufort"
)
#> `detection_data()`: 20 segments, 6 detections (m).
#>   g(0) = 1 is assumed; see `?detection_data`.
head(flat)
#> # A tibble: 6 × 9
#>   Region.Label  Area Sample.Label   Effort object distance  size distance_source
#>   <chr>        <dbl> <chr>           <dbl>  <int>    <dbl> <dbl> <chr>          
#> 1 all           5811 2024-04-01_2_1   7.78      1     229      1 angle          
#> 2 all           5811 2024-04-01_2_2   5.56      2     132.     2 angle          
#> 3 all           5811 2024-04-01_2_2   5.56      3     397.     1 angle          
#> 4 all           5811 2024-04-01_2_3   3.33     NA      NA     NA NA             
#> 5 all           5811 2024-04-01_2_4   5.56     NA      NA     NA NA             
#> 6 all           5811 2024-04-01_4_1   4.44     NA      NA     NA NA             
#> # ℹ 1 more variable: wt_beaufort <dbl>
library(Distance)

df <- ds(flat, key = "hn", truncation = "10%", formula = ~ wt_beaufort,
         convert_units = 0.001)   # distances in m, effort in km

summary(df)
plot(df)
gof_ds(df)

Points to note:

area is required and has no default. It scales abundance directly. The scripts this package was rewritten from had 5,811 km² written into the middle of a function, which is how a study-area figure outlives its study.

Segments with no detections are in the table, with a missing distance.

sum(is.na(flat$distance))
#> [1] 16

These rows are not padding. They record effort that produced no sightings. Dropping them removes part of the denominator and inflates density.

Use wt_beaufort, not mean_beaufort. wt_beaufort weights each record by the distance it covers, so a sea state held over 3 km counts for more than one recorded over 200 m. Detection depends on that quantity.

Circling detections are excluded by default, and the exclusion is reported. A position logged off the track is not measured at the moment of detection. The animals still count towards the segment’s abundance, so segs$sightings is unchanged. Excluding a detection from the detection function while counting it towards density is normal, and the two are separate arguments:

nrow(detection_data(segs, area = 5811, include_circling = TRUE))
#> `detection_data()`: 20 segments, 6 detections (m).
#>   g(0) = 1 is assumed; see `?detection_data`.
#> [1] 22

Check the source of each distance. The methods must state it, and point and interval distances cannot be fitted together:

table(flat$distance_source, useNA = "no")
#> 
#> angle 
#>     6

Truncation drops detections, not effort. The truncation argument of detection_data() drops detections beyond it and keeps their segments with effort intact: searched effort counts whether or not anything was seen within the truncation distance. Pass the same value to ds(). Otherwise the model is fitted to one set of detections and abundance is scaled by another.

nrow(detection_data(segs, area = 5811, truncation = 500))
#> `detection_data()`: 20 segments, 5 detections (m).
#>   dropped 1 beyond the truncation distance; their segments keep their effort
#>   g(0) = 1 is assumed; see `?detection_data`.
#> [1] 21

Compare models

Fitting a set of models and choosing the best has two traps.

AIC only compares models fitted to the same data. Changing the truncation changes which detections are in the likelihood, so AICs across truncations are not comparable. Vary key function, adjustments, and covariates at a fixed truncation. Compare truncations separately.

Binned and unbinned fits cannot share a table. STRIP distances are intervals and are fitted binned. Angle- and position-derived distances are points. A multi-year model set therefore splits along that line.

Rank on more than AIC. Abundance depends on the effective strip half-width, and two models within 2 AIC of each other can give materially different values of it. Report p‾\bar{p} (average detection probability) and its CV alongside AIC, with a goodness-of-fit statistic.

docs/07-fitting-architecture.md in the package repository covers this, where an automated model-selection sweep belongs, and what can and cannot be done about g(0).

Project the coordinates

mid_lon/mid_lat are decimal degrees. A smooth of longitude and latitude in degrees distorts distance at NARWC latitudes: at 43°N a degree of longitude is about 81 km, against 111 km for a degree of latitude. Project to an equal-area projection before modelling:

pts <- segments_as_sf(segs, "midpoints")

# Albers equal-area, Gulf of Maine
gom_aea <- paste(
  "+proj=aea +lat_1=40 +lat_2=46 +lat_0=43 +lon_0=-69",
  "+x_0=0 +y_0=0 +datum=WGS84 +units=km +no_defs"
)
projected <- sf::st_transform(pts, gom_aea)

xy <- sf::st_coordinates(projected)
head(xy)
#>              X         Y
#> [1,]  0.000000  3.893573
#> [2,]  0.000000 10.568327
#> [3,]  0.000000 15.018201
#> [4,]  0.000000 19.468104
#> [5,] -8.107262 30.041539
#> [6,] -8.102634 33.935268

Build the dsm inputs

dsm needs two data frames with fixed column names. They map directly from distsamp output:

library(dsm)

segment.data <- data.frame(
  Sample.Label = segs$segments$seg_id,
  Effort       = segs$segments$seg_eff,   # km
  X            = xy[, 1],                 # projected, km
  Y            = xy[, 2],
  beaufort     = segs$segments$wt_beaufort
)

# The detections the detection function was actually fitted to, after
# truncation, so `object` matches.
fitted <- df$ddf$data
observation.data <- data.frame(
  object       = fitted$object,
  Sample.Label = fitted$Sample.Label,
  size         = fitted$size,
  distance     = fitted$distance
)

object is the detection identifier from detection_data(). dsm uses it to link each detection to its row in the fitted detection function. Taking the rows from df$ddf$data keeps the two consistent after truncation.

Add covariates

distsamp gives each segment a location and nothing else. Environmental covariates, such as depth, sea surface temperature (SST), and fronts, must be sampled at each segment midpoint by the user. segments_as_sf(segs, "midpoints") is the intended handoff:

pts <- segments_as_sf(segs, "midpoints")

# e.g. with terra
depth <- terra::extract(bathymetry_raster, terra::vect(pts))
segment.data$depth <- depth[, 2]

Sample at the midpoint, as Becker et al. (2019) do: covariates “derived based on the segment’s geographical mid-point”, with SST and depth standard deviations taken over a 3 × 3-pixel box around it. segment_midpoints() places the midpoint half the segment’s effort along the track, not at the centroid of its records, so it lies on the trackline.

Match covariates in time as well as space. A segment flown in April needs April’s SST, not the annual mean. segs$segments$DATE holds the survey date for this.

Fit the density surface model 

mod <- dsm(
  count ~ s(X, Y, bs = "ts") + s(depth, bs = "ts"),
  ddf.obj = df,
  segment.data = segment.data,
  observation.data = observation.data,
  family = tw(),          # Tweedie handles the zero inflation
  method = "REML",
  convert.units = 0.001   # distances in m, effort in km
)

summary(mod)
plot(mod)
gam.check(mod)

A Tweedie or negative binomial family is usually appropriate: most segments hold no animals, and the non-zero counts are overdispersed. Miller et al. (2013) discuss the choice.

Report the settings

Record the seed. Without it the segmentation is not reproducible, and neither is anything downstream.

str(segs$settings)
#> List of 13
#>  $ seg_length         : num 5
#>  $ species            : chr "RIWH"
#>  $ seed               : num 1
#>  $ seg_tol_frac       : num 0.5
#>  $ min_track_km       : num 1
#>  $ min_segment_km     : num 1
#>  $ dist_method        : chr "haversine"
#>  $ circling           : chr "same_species"
#>  $ circling_distance  : chr "with_group"
#>  $ circling_max_gap_km: num 5
#>  $ distance_units     : chr "m"
#>  $ platform           : chr "aerial"
#>  $ distance_sources   : chr [1:3] "angle" "exact" "strip"

Suggested methods wording is in docs/06-references.md in the package repository.
